description: Owner-locked 20 atomic test claims for Truth Auditor calibration

claims.atomic_claim: Small geometric clay objects surviving from Late Uruk administrative levels exist in forms such as spheres, cones, disks, and cylinders between 1 and 3 cm in dimension.
Catalogue object OIM A64678 is a broken clay envelope from Chogha Mish measuring 7.8 by 7.2 cm that preserves clay tokens inside.
Exterior marks on some hollow clay envelopes allowed administrators to inspect enclosed quantities without immediately opening the envelope.
Impressed cylinder-seal rollings on clay media functioned to mark an association with authority, custody or witnessing.
In a representative manufacturing workflow, an administrative operator deposited clay counters into moist clay, closed the envelope, marked and sealed its exterior, and let it dry.
In a representative sealing practice, an operator bound a closure with cord, pressed moist clay over it and rolled a seal, such that later access broke the clay.
Numerical tablet fragment ChM III-937a was created to record the exact transaction previously secured by hollow envelope OIM A64678.
Cylinder seals were rolled across clay envelopes specifically to bind communal responsibility among Sumerian village elders.
Hollow clay bullae were invented specifically to prevent fraud and theft during the long-distance transport of goods.
Chogha Mish envelope OIM A64678 was manufactured because an administrator distrusted an illiterate shepherd delivering sheep.
The rapid physical expansion of Uruk caused human administrative memory to collapse, which directly produced the invention of clay tokens.
The inconvenience of having to break hollow clay envelopes in order to verify contents caused accountants to abandon envelopes and invent flat numerical tablets.
All hollow clay envelopes bear exterior stylus impressions reflecting the exact quantity and shapes of the tokens enclosed inside.
Geometric clay tokens formed a single, universally standardized accounting code across all prehistoric Near Eastern settlements for 5,000 years.

Administrative recording evolved through an obligatory developmental sequence: loose tokens were placed into hollow envelopes, which led to surface impressions, which evolved into solid numerical tablets, which finally became proto-cuneiform.
The appearance of flat numerical tablets immediately and completely replaced the use of hollow envelopes and loose tokens across southern Mesopotamia.
Late Uruk geometric clay tokens themselves do not carry written phonetic language or transcribe human speech.
Surviving proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk IV do not record continuous spoken discourse, poetry, or historical narrative.

Surviving rounded and semi-circular depressions on Late Uruk clay tablets were produced by carved reed styluses, though the wooden and reed tools themselves rarely survive in the archaeological record.

During the late fourth millennium BCE in southern Mesopotamia, there was an administrative shift toward direct surface recording on clay, but this shift took place alongside overlapping earlier clay practices rather than through a single invention event.
